AGUI (Agent–User Interaction Protocol) is an open, lightweight, eventbased standard designed to connect AI agents to userfacing applications across web, mobile, terminals, and chat platforms.[1]



 Core Purpose

Traditional requestandresponse architectures (like standard REST or GraphQL APIs) struggle with agentic workflows that require multiturn streaming, shared state, clientside actions, and human intervention.[1]

AGUI standardizes how agent runtime events, UI intents, and user interactions flow bidirectionally between backends and frontends without adhoc custom wiring.[1]



 The Agentic Protocol Ecosystem

AGUI is part of a broader standard stack for agentic computing:[1]

| Layer | Protocol / Standard | Focus & Role |
| : | : | : |
| Agent ↔ User | AGUI | Connects agents to user interfaces for realtime interaction and state [1]. |
| Agent ↔ Tools & Data | MCP (Model Context Protocol) | Connects agents securely to external databases, tools, and APIs [1]. |
| Agent ↔ Agent | A2A (Agent to Agent) | Orchestrates distributed coordination across distinct agents [1]. |



 Key Capabilities & Features

 Streaming and Multimodality: Realtime token and event streaming, typed file attachments, voice, and media playback.[1]
 Generative UI: Delivers structured outputs to render typed UI components or declarative interface trees.[1]
 Shared State: Synchronizes typed state bidirectionally between the user interface and backend using event diffs.[1]
 HumanintheLoop Interrupts: Supports pausing executions for user approvals, manual edits, or steerable interventions midflow.[1]
 Frontend & Backend Tooling: Manages typed execution handoffs between agent backend tools and clientside actions.[1]



 Supported Ecosystem & Integrations

The protocol was originated by the team behind  and supports a wide range of frameworks and environments:[1]

 Frameworks: LangGraph, CrewAI, Agno, Pydantic AI, Mastra, LlamaIndex, AG2, Microsoft Agent Framework, Google ADK, and Claude Managed Agents.[1]
 Infrastructure: Native deployment support in runtimes such as .[2]
 SDKs & Clients: Multilanguage SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Dart) and client integrations spanning Web, Slack, Microsoft Teams, and CLI terminals.[1]
